claims.text: High-temperature stability of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles is governed by configurational-entropy stabilization.
Highly synergistic intermetallic bonding suppresses atomic diffusion and phase segregation in these nanoparticles.
Disrupting the near-equiatomic composition reduces entropy stabilization.
Reduced entropy stabilization initiates elemental segregation or phase separation under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
Near-equiatomic intermixing produces atomic-scale disorder and lattice distortions.
Atomic-scale disorder and lattice distortions create high configurational entropy.
The proposed disorder, lattice distortion, configurational entropy, and bonding mediate resistance to phase segregation.
Configurational entropy lowers the free energy of the homogeneous alloy and thereby provides a thermodynamic barrier to phase separation.
Synergistic intermetallic interactions restrict atomic mobility at high temperature.
Moving away from equiatomic balance makes the nanoparticles more prone to diffusion-driven segregation and phase decomposition.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, equiatomic nanoparticles will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure and compositional uniformity.
Off-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit more phase decomposition than equiatomic nanoparticles under the same conditions.
Possible manifestations of off-equiatomic decomposition include elemental segregation, noble-metal surface enrichment, and secondary-phase formation.
The effect is sensitive to elemental combination, particle size, processing history, and the time and energy available for atomic rearrangement.
Instability-onset temperatures and segregation extent may vary among alloy compositions.
Kinetic barriers may delay observable decomposition even when decomposition is thermodynamically favorable.
